vignette:
Adekunle sits in the therapy room, his posture a study in contained tension. At 23, he is a recent graduate, a promising urban planner whose career was just beginning to take shape six months ago. Now, he describes his life as if viewing it through warped glass. The world he once navigated with confidence has become a landscape of hidden threats. It all began on a mild autumn night, walking home from a friend's birthday celebration. He remembers the sharp, sweet smell of spilled whiskey on the pavement first, then the voices—loud, slurring, and angry. A small group of men blocked his path. He tried to step around them, but the anger in the air was thick and volatile. He cannot recall the sequence of events with any clarity; when he tries, his memory serves up only a series of stark, silent photographs. There is the image of a man's face, contorted in a voiceless shout. There is another of a green glass bottle held aloft, catching the streetlight. And the final, most vivid snapshot: the starburst of shattering glass on the brick wall just past his head. The memory comes with no sound, only a wave of pure, overwhelming terror that floods his body and forces him to shut his mind down. He knows what happened, but when he attempts to form the words, his throat tightens, the narrative dissolving before he can grasp it.

In the weeks that followed, Adekunle believed he could simply move on. But the city he was paid to redesign now felt menacing. At his open-plan office, the sudden slam of a door down the hall can make him jump in his seat, heart hammering against his ribs. A colleague casually tossing a wadded-up piece of paper into a bin across the room caused him to flinch so violently he knocked over his coffee. The sudden movement of someone walking up behind his desk provokes a full-body jolt, a surge of adrenaline that leaves him trembling and ashamed. He has come to believe that he is fundamentally incapable of dealing with even the slightest upset. This conviction plays out most painfully in his work. Urban planning is a field of competing interests and necessary debate, but Adekunle now avoids any situation that might hold a whisper of confrontation. During a recent community feedback session for a new pedestrian plaza, a local business owner voiced a calm but firm objection to his proposed layout. Instead of defending his meticulously researched plan, Adekunle felt a familiar wave of panic rise in his chest. He conceded the point immediately, his silence and quick capitulation earning him a confused look from his project manager. The people who should have protected him that night—the police who arrived late and took a dismissive report—had let him down, and this has curdled into a deeper certainty that he is utterly helpless, that he alone must prevent bad things from happening by avoiding any and all conflict.

His nights are the worst. Alone in his apartment, the locked door offers no comfort against the feeling of imminent danger. He finds it impossible to believe he is truly safe. His mind circles endlessly, replaying the assault not as it was, but as it could have been. He dwells on what he did wrong: he shouldn't have taken that route, he should have seen them sooner, he should have said something different to de-escalate. The self-blame is a relentless hum beneath the surface of his thoughts. To escape it, he turns to his phone, losing himself for hours in the bright, frictionless world of online sports betting. The brief, sharp thrill of a potential win is the only thing that can temporarily silence the fear and the shame. It is a fleeting and expensive reprieve. He finally sought help after visiting a friend to watch a football game. When their team fumbled a crucial play, his friend swore and threw a sofa cushion at the floor in frustration. The sight of the object flying through the air, combined with his friend's flash of anger, plunged Adekunle into a state of silent terror so profound he had to leave without explanation. He is here now because he cannot continue to live this way, yet he is haunted by the fear that revisiting the memory, that trying to find the words, will only prove what he already suspects: that he is broken beyond repair.
